newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia posts trade deficit in April.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia posts trade deficit in April.

text.p: Malaysia on Friday announced a monthly trade deficit in April of 2.1 billion ringgit ($836 million) after a 1.75 billion ringgit surplus in March, with items such as planes and boats driving up the import bill.
The Statistics Department said on Friday exports dropped 16.2 percent month-on-month to 15.7 billion ringgit, mostly due to declines in commodity and oil earnings.
Imports rose 5.1 percent to 17.8 billion ringgit, mainly due to purchases of aircraft, ships and floating structures for the oil industry.
The cumulative deficit for the first four months of the year was 109.5 million ringgit, substantially lower than the 1.6 billion ringgit deficit in the same period of 1996.
But it was the first time exports have contracted this year.
Rubber export earnings led the decline, dropping by 316.2 million ringgit from March. Oil earnings fell by 137.9 million ringgit and saw logs and sawn timber dropped 162.2 million.
Economists predicted Malaysia's trade account would continue to show a deficit for the year, partly due to a stronger yen, weaker commodity prices and slower growth in key manufactured exports.
"We are expecting the yen to strengthen in the third quarter so the monthly trade data should go into deficit," said Dilip Ratha, senior economist at Singapore's W.I. Carr.
"Exports are definitely weaker than expected," said Andy Tan, General Manager of MMS International in Singapore.

"We had been expecting some growth in that area. But it would appear that the declines were mostly in commodities and oil earnings. It would be more worrisome if there was decline in manufactured exports.
"We shouldn't be unduly alarmed by the picture in April," Tan said, adding that the cumulative deficit so far was in line with his forecast of a 1.0 billion ringgit deficit for the year.
Daniel Lian, regional economist at Natwest Markets, said that April's deficit was within expectations.
"Overall, trade numbers in Malaysia still look good. We are maintaining our projection of a trade deficit of about two billion ringgit for the year," he said.
Franklin Tan, head of research at Y.K. Fung Securities, said much of the increase in imports was due to purchases of capital goods, a healthy sign in a growing economy.
"There was a lot of imports of capital goods, mainly driven by last year's high manufacturing approvals. These (approvals) rose around 30 to 40 percent last year," Tan said.

"The growth in capital goods imports will continue to rise over the next few months. The question the market is asking is when will exports turn? I think it will be three to six months before we have a turnaround in exports," he said.

Kevin Chew, economist at Caspian Securities, said the market is looking to see if growth picks up in the key electrical and electronics sector, which account for around half of Malaysia's export earnings.

"Exports in April were quite weak, showing the first contraction since December. But they have been weak since the middle of 1996. I think expectations are geared to the second half, with a stronger recovery in the electronics sector.
"You've got good months and bad months," Chew said.
($1 = 2.51 ringgit)
